newsitem.title: USA: Kemp and Democrats trade ideas on cities.
newsitem.headline: Kemp and Democrats trade ideas on cities.

text.p: Republican vice-presidential candidate Jack Kemp brought his message of urban renewal and tax cuts to New York on Friday but a group of Democratic mayors accused his party of blocking his ideas for the cities.

Kemp said that under an administration led by Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, public housing projects would not be "blown up," a reference to the practice of destroying decaying apartment blocks in big cities.

"If we sold it to the residents and allowed them to form a resident co-op through a management corporation, they would own equity in the building and in their apartment," Kemp told a meeting of the Association for a Better New York attended by business and union leaders. "When people own something they treat it differently than when they don't."

At a sidewalk news conference to respond to Kemp's remarks, the mayors of Philadelphia, Baltimore, East Orange, New Jersey and New York City Council Speaker Peter Vallone said the Dole-Kemp campaign's 15 percent tax cut plan would hurt cities and urged urban dwellers to vote for President Clinton.

"Cities would be ripped asunder by that tax cut, programme after programme, even the crime bill, which has been so succesful, would get ripped apart by that tax cut," Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell said.
Vallone said that "while we admire much of what Jack Kemp said today the best question asked (from the audience) was 'are you sure Mr Kemp that you're in the right party?'."

Rendell said that when Kemp was Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in the Bush administration his plans to create enterprise zones and help low-income city families were stopped by his Republican Party.
In his remarks, Kemp said a new administration would "get rid of the 83-year-old tax code...to unleash the talent of America."
He said capital needed to be created to flow down into struggling urban centres. "We can't go into the 21st century leaving anyone behind."
Kemp arrived in New York Thursday to attend a dinner hosted by Roman Catholic Cardinal John O'Connor along with his opponent in the November 5 election, Vice President Al Gore.
